item.title: Holiday spending heralds upbeat start to 4th quarter
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
Holiday spending heralds upbeat start to 4th quarter Strong show by trade-in program boosts sentiment Brisk spending during the ongoing National Day holiday in China has made for an encouraging start to the fourth quarter, with continued policy support expected to sustain the improvement in consumer demand in the months ahead, experts said on Monday. Data from the Ministry of Commerce showed that during the first three days of the holiday (Oct 1-3), sales at 78 pedestrian shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the ministry rose 5.3 percent year-on-year, outpacing a 3.4 percent increase in the number of visitors. The consumer goods trade-in program generated another positive snapshot, supporting 19.63 billion yuan ($2.93 billion) in sales during the period. Under the program, automobile trade-ins totaled 46,000 vehicles, driving 7.45 billion yuan in new car sales; home appliances trade-ins reached 1.51 million units, generating 6.5 billion yuan; and digital and smart product purchases hit 1.709 million units, contributing 4.9 billion yuan, according to the ministry. Offshore duty-free shopping also put up a strong showing. According to Haikou Customs, from Oct 1 to 3, duty-free sales totaled 358 million yuan in Hainan province, with 55,100 shoppers purchasing 277,000 items, an increase of 8.85 percent, 12.9 percent and 8 percent, respectively, compared with the same period in 2025. Zhou Mi, a senior researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, said the holiday spending was driven by a strong consumer willingness to purchase. He said the growth in services consumption marks a market upgrade, as it is a sign of a mature consumption market structure. "There is a stronger demand for innovative products, as China's vast population has a growing appetite for smarter shopping experiences," Zhou said. For example, at the Lanzhou International Auto Show held in Lanzhou, Gansu province, during the holiday, intelligent features were on full display. New energy vehicles integrated with AI drew particular attention. "Please activate the driver and passenger seat massage!""What's the altitude here?" visitors could be heard asking as they interacted with in-car AI systems, experiencing advanced intelligent driving assistance. Zhang Shuwei, head of the organizing committee, said over 70 brands and 120 dealerships participated in the event, held in a space covering more than 40,000 square meters. A combination of cutting-edge products and subsidies from dealers and manufacturers allowed buyers to compare their options and place orders on-site. Liu Ying, a researcher at Renmin University of China's Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, said the holiday consumption data "demonstrates China's economic vitality and domestic demand potential". According to Liu, the figures point to an encouraging start to the fourth quarter, and the broader challenge would be to translate concentrated holiday demand into sustained household spending. Government support for purchases and opportunities in service consumption offer scope for growth, she added. For the fourth quarter, one concrete source of support is the latest allocation of trade-in funding. The National Development and Reform Commission said on Sept 30 that a fourth batch of 62.5 billion yuan in ultra-long special treasury bond funds had been allocated to local governments, bringing the full-year allocation for consumer goods trade-ins to 250 billion yuan. The funding provides a basis for continued subsidies through the year-end shopping season, which could be a strong catalyst for accelerated consumption, experts added. Though the full third-quarter figures are yet to be released, latest available data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed that retail sales rose 1.1 percent year-on-year in the first eight months, with growth of 0.4 percent in August. "A more durable consumption expansion will depend on improvements in employment and income expectations, alongside businesses' ability to meet changing consumer needs," Liu said. masi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: English changed his life and then that of others
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
English changed his life and then that of others Ou Wen's first encounter with English dates to the Chairman Mao era. He was 8 years old, barefoot and standing in the cold dirt of a village in Hunan province, when a cousin took an English textbook from his schoolbag and began reading from it, "I love Peking's Tian'anmen". Ou had no idea what the words meant. His cousin, who knew several English words, seemed to possess a mysterious power. "From that moment," Ou recalled recently, "I said to myself, I must learn English." His English name, Owen, sounds exactly like his Chinese name. This was an inconvenient ambition for a boy in rural China in the 1970s. His middle school, run by the local people's commune, did not teach English. When Ou first tried to enter high school, he failed. He was particularly bad at the one subject he most wanted to learn. He eventually passed the entrance exam one year later. At his new school, he discovered that passing an exam and knowing English were two different things. He could memorize grammar. He could not understand what his teacher was saying. At the time, English lessons were broadcast over the radio. A transistor receiver cost eighteen yuan ($2.68), about half his father's monthly salary. Ou calculated that there was only one way to afford it. He would stop eating breakfast. For three months, he drank a glass of water every morning and went to school hungry. On holidays, he walked 60 kilometers home rather than spend a little more than one yuan on a bus ticket. Eventually he had enough money for the radio. The radio eventually led him to Mike Lane, a teacher from the United States at a local college. Ou began sitting in on Mike's classes. For almost a year, he bicycled an hour each way to attend. Mostly, he understood nothing. Then, one Thanksgiving evening in November 1985, he did. "Suddenly I wasn't translating in my head anymore," Ou said. "I was just — understanding." By then he had graduated from a three-year technical school in "aquatic production" and was working for a fisheries administrative office in Hengyang. His job was, essentially, counting fish catches, writing reports and presumably acquiring a reasonable familiarity with the administrative life of freshwater creatures. But English remained his private obsession. He went to the railway station to talk to foreigners. He carried vocabulary cards in his trouser pocket. He wrote English words on his palms. He began printing membership forms for something called the Hengyang English Lovers Association. The turning point was in 1987 when Ou went to Yangshuo, the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, an international tourist site famous for its karst landscape. Ou was surprised by something else. At a fruit stall, he saw local farmers bargaining with tourists in English. Ou had spent years trying to manufacture opportunities to speak English. In Yangshuo, the opportunities were standing in the street. He became an English guide and later a hotel receptionist. He taught Chinese to a Danish traveler for ten yuan an hour, which struck him as a spectacular sum. Gradually, he began to understand something that textbooks had not been able to teach him: English was useful. "In Yangshuo," he said, "I saw the value of English with my own eyes." In 1993, after several unsuccessful ventures in Hainan island, Ou founded Buckland, one of Yangshuo's first private foreign-language schools. His students were mostly rural teenagers who had failed their high-school entrance examinations. Ou recognized them immediately. They were, in various ways, the people he had once been. His teaching method was not complicated. He wanted the students to talk. Foreign teachers were brought into classrooms. Students were sent into the streets to guide tourists. Grammar, which had once occupied so much of Ou's own education, was given less authority. The school has expanded over the past decades. Buckland has trained nearly 1,000 foreign teachers for over 100 schools across China, and taught English to countless local people. "Over the years, I've seen that he genuinely wants to teach those who come to China, and truly enjoys it," said Clinton Moore, a US citizen and a student of Ou, who has been living in China since 2010. "Ou has helped give me better understanding about China and its people." "English changed my fate," Ou said. "But it also changed the fate of many others." He paused. "That is the part that matters." Li Ziyu in Guilin contributed to this story.

item.title: Chongqing home preserves revolutionary history
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
Chongqing home preserves revolutionary history To mark the start of the autumn semester in early September, 630 primary and secondary school students and teachers from Chongqing's Pengshui Miao and Tujia autonomous county visited a century-old residence in the Huangjia township, where they listened to captivating stories of the Red Army's journey during the Long March. The sanheyuan, or three-sided courtyard house, belonged to the late Huang Xuezhen who was a villager in the Xianfeng community of Huangjia. It has since been transformed into the Chongqing Red Army Historical Museum, where stories of perseverance are told through its preserved bricks and tiles, and most notably, a "Red Army message slip" that has been cherished for 92 years. "Through this firsthand visit, I understand the hardships during the Long March and the greatness of our predecessors, which deeply moved and inspired me," said Zou Siyi, a first-year secondary school student. The Long March, a monumental 12,500-kilometer expedition, is a pivotal event in Chinese history. It not only marked the Communist Party of China's strategic transfer but also exemplified the profound bond between the army and the people. In 1934, when the Red Army passed through Huangjia, local villagers, misled by reactionary propaganda, sought refuge in the mountains. The soldiers, in need of sustenance, entered Huang's house, consumed half a jar of pickled vegetables and used some firewood. Before departing, they replenished the water tank, tidied up the room, and left six liters of soybeans as compensation, along with a note explaining their actions. "Boss: We ate half a jar of your pickled vegetables, a few green onions, and burned a few sticks of firewood. In compensation, we have left you with six liters of soybeans," read the note. Huang secretly preserved the note as a testament to the Red Army's integrity and connection to the people. In 1958, it was presented to the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution as a first-class cultural relic. Today, the museum serves as a national defense and Party history education base. It is also part of a broader effort by the local government to develop historical sites, including the Red Army Street and a martyrs' cemetery, to honor the region's rich Red culture. "Throughout the year, particularly from June to August, the area hosts Party-building activities and student programs, where participants engage with local communities and learn about revolutionary history," said Zhang Xingxing, an employee of the township government. The township's "First Lesson of the School Year" and "Retracing the Red Army's Path" programs, now in their ninth year, combine revolutionary history with legal education, inspiring students to appreciate their heritage and work hard in the new school year. "The number of visitors is quite impressive for our remote township since we started developing tourism in 2012, though visitors have to endure long, winding mountain roads," said Huang Qinghua, Party secretary of the Xianfeng community. The community has welcomed an average of about 30,000 tourists annually, with operational income reaching 980,000 yuan ($146,086)over the past three years, he said. Pengshui, located in the southeast of Chongqing, is home to 318,000 Miao people who make up 45.4 percent of the county's population. According to local authorities, it has the largest concentration of Miao people in all ethnic minority counties. Huang Qinghua added that in recent years, his township has focused on developing an eco-industrial area by leveraging its Red cultural heritage and local Miao customs. Contact the writers at dengrui@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Coffee majors rewriting playbook in China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
Coffee majors rewriting playbook in China Investors paying less attention to how many outlets open, increasingly focused on whether stores generate healthy profits For much of the past decade, success in China's coffee market was measured by two numbers: how many stores a company could open and how cheaply it could sell a cup of joe. That formula helped transform China into one of the world's fastest-growing coffee markets. Chains rushed to blanket cities with outlets, expanded into counties and townships and conditioned consumers to expect coffee for as little as 9.9 yuan ($1.47) a cup. Now, the industry's biggest players are rewriting the playbook. Rather than chasing store counts at all costs, companies from Starbucks China to Luckin Coffee are increasingly emphasizing store productivity, premium experiences and sustainable returns, reflecting a broader shift as China's coffee market enters a more mature stage of development. The transition marks an important inflection point for an industry that has spent years prioritizing scale over efficiency. As store networks become denser and competition intensifies, investors are paying less attention to how many outlets companies open and more attention to whether those stores generate healthy profits. No company better illustrates the shift than Starbucks China. In September, Starbucks opened its new-generation flagship Starbucks Reserve inside Beijing SKP, one of China's most prestigious luxury shopping malls. Far more than another coffee shop, the location serves as a showcase for Starbucks' evolving strategy. The store combines Reserve coffee, Italian desserts and the national debut of its "Global Inspiration" gifting collection, aiming to create a destination where coffee, luxury retail and lifestyle experiences converge. The concept represents Starbucks' "thousands of stores, thousands of faces" strategy. Stores are increasingly customized according to local neighborhoods, shopping districts and customer occasions, instead of following a standardized global format. "Starbucks Reserve is an innovative practice in which we respond to customer needs and the character of the trade area, using creativity, professional capability and global resources to create a distinctive experience," said Molly Liu, CEO of Starbucks China. "It is also an important exploration under our 'thousands of stores, thousands of faces' strategy — co-creating a destination space with a landmark retail partner." The strategy comes just months after Starbucks Global completed its strategic partnership with Boyu Capital, which also owns SKP. The investment has accelerated Starbucks China's transition toward what executives describe as a "high-quality, scenario-based" expansion strategy. The company is tailoring formats to different consumption occasions, including premium commercial landmarks, lower-tier cities, cultural tourism destinations and everyday neighborhood locations. As of Sept 15, Starbucks operated 8,238 stores across China. During fiscal 2026, it added 227 net new stores while entering 69 county-level markets. Nearly half of those openings were in third-tier cities and smaller markets, where management said new-store profitability has remained strong. Luckin Coffee, China's largest coffee chain by store count, is taking a different route toward the same objective. Unlike Starbucks, Luckin continues to expand aggressively. But executives are increasingly emphasizing operating quality alongside expansion. The company reported second-quarter revenue of 15.89 billion yuan, up 28.5 percent from a year earlier, while operating profit rose 22 percent to 2.12 billion yuan. Company-run store operating margins remained above 21 percent despite continued promotional activity.

item.title: Ceramic paradise in Jingdezhen
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
Ceramic paradise in Jingdezhen A foreign artist and his daughter build a life in China's renowned "porcelain capital" Working in the Sanbao International Ceramic Art Village in Jingdezhen, Jiangxi province, Wisam Al-Samad, an Iraqi-born, Norway-based artist from the International Academy of Ceramics, is one of thousands of foreign artists who have become known as "foreign Jingdezhen drifters" (yang jing piao). During his first visit to China, he moved to the village with his daughter Zahra to begin an artistic residency. After one and a half months of painstaking work, he finished his ceramic mural Love — The End of the World. Made up of 45 ceramic panels symbolizing love and passion, the artwork blends elements of ancient Mesopotamian civilization, Norway's aurora-lit landscapes and Jingdezhen's local clay and time-honored kiln techniques. Using ceramics as a bridge and universal love as its language, the piece crosses divides of nationality, religion and culture. Away from urban noise, Sanbao village provides the artist with a quiet creative space and abundant resources, alongside a simple, warm rural life. When working, Al-Samad focuses on throwing clay, tending kilns and polishing artworks. In his free time, he wanders through tea gardens, admires antique pottery and enjoys pastoral moments with Zahra. Immersed in Chinese tea culture and countryside charm, the father and daughter are crafting a touching story of cross-cultural artistic connection in China's renowned "porcelain capital". item.title: Logistics base boosts Sino-Central Asian connectivity
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
Logistics base boosts Sino-Central Asian connectivity Cooperation hub integrates services, warehousing and transport modes The first tangible project of the Belt and Road Initiative, the China-Kazakhstan (Lianyungang) Logistics Cooperation Base, was officially inaugurated on May 19,2014. After more than a decade of operation, the base in eastern China's Jiangsu province has become an international economic platform for warehousing, logistics and trade, serving Central Asian countries and playing a key role in enhancing connectivity between China and Central Asia. The base was officially inaugurated in the presence of the heads of state of China and Kazakhstan. The site now operates a 220,000-square-meter container yard with 1,763 container berths and a 3.8-kilometer dedicated railway spur, with an annual handling capacity of up to 410,000 20-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, said Zhao Duofa, general manager of China-Kazakhstan (Lianyungang)International Logistics. As the sole loading and unloading terminal for Lianyungang's international freight trains, the company has launched services along routes connecting China with the five Central Asian countries and Turkiye, Russia, Europe and Mongolia. Zhao added that the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway has also been smoothly constructed. "To date, the company has operated more than 8,000 international freight trains. Since Lianyungang launched its international freight train service in 1992, the total number of trains operated has exceeded 18,000," Zhao added. As the first tangible project to be implemented following the launch of the BRI, the China-Kazakhstan (Lianyungang) Logistics Cooperation Base also embodies the aspirations of Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries for access to the sea via an eastern route. Zhao said that, from its initial focus on infrastructure and logistics cooperation the base has expanded collaboration in trade, industry and supply chains. It has evolved from a transshipment station for international freight trains into a comprehensive logistics hub integrating container terminals, end-to-end agency services, warehousing and logistics, and multimodal transport, he said. The base currently deals with westbound shipments of electronics, machinery parts, daily necessities, used cars and chemical products, as well as eastbound shipments of wheat, ferroalloys and potash fertilizer. It handles more than 50 percent of China's westbound transit cargo. "More than 80 percent of daily consumer goods imported from China via Kazakhstan, along with key Kazakh exports such as mineral products and grain, are consolidated and distributed through Lianyungang Port, helping to establish a balanced 'round-trip' flow of international freight trains," the general manager said. Bedelov Azilkhan, deputy general manager of China-Kazakhstan (Lianyungang) International Logistics, said in the past, Kazakhstan's wheat was mainly exported to China and neighboring Central Asian countries. Reaching more distant markets was a major challenge due to long transport routes, lengthy transit times and high costs. "With the logistics hub in place, Kazakh wheat and other agricultural products can now be transported to China via the China-Europe (Central Asia) Railway Express and, from there, shipped onward to third-party markets," he added. In the early days, trade was dominated by clothing, toys and daily necessities. Today, the range of goods has expanded to include automobiles, auto parts, home appliances and photovoltaic modules, reflecting the growing integration of China's advanced manufacturing capabilities with markets in Central Asia, Bedelov said. "An even more noticeable change is that the flow of goods is no longer one-way. Whereas Chinese goods were once the only shipments to Central Asia, agricultural products such as Kazakh wheat, along with mineral products, can now enter China smoothly and be shipped onward to other markets," he said. In the first half of 2026, rail freight between Kazakhstan and China reached 18.7 million metric tons, up 9 percent year-on-year. Of that total, 11.7 million tons moved from Kazakhstan to China, with Kazakhstan's rail exports to China rising 20 percent to 8.5 million tons. The cargo included ores, grain and other agricultural products, ferrous and non-ferrous metals, petroleum products and other commodities. Bilateral trade has also continued to expand. According to Kazakhstan's Ministry of Trade and Integration, trade between the two countries reached $32.4 billion in the first seven months of 2026, up 24.1 percent year-on-year. "The growing two-way flow through Lianyungang is important not simply because more goods are moving in both directions. It shows that the logic of cooperation is evolving from infrastructure connectivity toward productive and supply-chain integration," said Gulnar Shaimergenova, founder and director of the China Studies Center (Kazakhstan). For Kazakhstan, the "landlocked country plus seaport" model demonstrates that geography does not have to determine economic destiny, she said. "The traditional disadvantage of being a landlocked country is not simply the absence of a coastline. It is the dependence on other countries' infrastructure, ports and transit decisions. Kazakhstan's response has been to build a diversified logistics network in which we increasingly participate not only as a cargo owner, but also as an infrastructure partner and logistics operator," she added. Broader transformation She said Lianyungang is a good microcosm of the broader transformation because the project itself has evolved from a transport facility into a platform connecting logistics, trade, digital services, green technologies and regional supply chains. "Kazakhstan therefore benefits from what I would call a portfolio of transport corridors," Gulnar said. "The Middle Corridor (Trans-Caspian International Transport Route)connects us with the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus, Turkiye and Europe. China-Europe (Central Asia) rail services link Kazakhstan directly with China's transport network. North-South routes provide access to Iran and the Gulf, while new southern routes are expanding the options available to businesses across Central Asia," she added. The China-Kazakhstan (Lianyungang) Logistics Cooperation Base has gradually evolved from a single logistics hub into a key transport corridor linking China's eastern coast with Central Asia and, ultimately, Europe, said Lu Yang, deputy director of the Institute of Economy and Finance of the School of Marxism at Tsinghua University. Its development has taken on growing significance for China-Kazakhstan cooperation and for broader connectivity and economic cooperation between China and Central Asia, she said. Practical model The base has become a practical model for connecting China's coastal ports with the landlocked countries of Central Asia. By providing access to the sea through China's eastern ports, it helps address the logistical constraints associated with being landlocked and offers a model that other Central Asian countries can draw on, she said. It has also strengthened connectivity between China and the Central Asian countries, contributing to deeper economic cooperation and the building of a China-Central Asia community with a shared future, Lu added. "Through land-sea transport corridors, Central Asia is no longer confined to its traditional regional trade networks, but is gaining greater access to global markets and becoming more closely integrated into the global trade system," she said. Lu pointed out that the value of the base has long extended beyond the basic function of "transporting goods". It is evolving into comprehensive platforms for cooperation, facilitating trade, strengthening industrial and supply chain links, and promoting people-to-people exchanges. In terms of trade facilitation, the base has promoted practical cooperation between China and Kazakhstan in areas such as customs clearance, inspection and quarantine, and transit regulations. It has also strengthened collaboration at border crossings, streamlined cross-border procedures and accumulated practical experience in the clearance of cross-border cargo, she said. At the industrial and supply chain level, the Lianyungang base has leveraged its logistics hub function to facilitate the development of warehousing and processing facilities, cross-border distribution networks and trading platforms. Chinese and Central Asian enterprises can connect supply with demand here, promoting the integration of resources, production capacity and markets, Lu said. In terms of people-to-people exchanges, the project has facilitated the movement of businesspeople, technical personnel and managers between the two countries. As commercial cooperation has expanded, so too have people-to-people interactions, making the base a window through which the two sides can better understand each other, she said. liujianqiao@chinadaily.cm.cn

item.title: Young riders' grit on tracks
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Young riders' grit on tracks Youth motocross builds resilience and discipline amid growing popularity At the 2026 FIM World Superbike Championship, Chinese motorcycle startup ZXMOTO secured five historic wins, drawing global attention to the rapid rise of China's motorcycle racing prowess. On Beijing's off-road tracks, young riders chase their dreams amid dust and engine roars, learning resilience through falls and forging strength at high speed. They emerge as the inspiring new generation in China's youth motocross scene. Xuanxuan, a third-grade pupil, began motocross training at six on a 50cc motorcycle. Four years of rigorous weekend training taught him corner control, obstacle navigation and jump techniques. "Flying over that jump makes me feel so free; it makes all the hard work worthwhile," he says. Although he had cried minutes earlier after spraining his ankle, he lit up when talking about what he loves.

item.title: Serving up an ace cultural experience
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Serving up an ace cultural experience Stars immerse themselves in Beijing's traditional, and trendy, activities A trip without a dip into the profound culture is never a complete China Open experience, and tennis' top stars are enjoying a break from the grueling season to soak up Beijing's rich history and tradition. With world-class facilities, top services and highest prize money in Asia on offer, the China Open never disappoints when it comes to delivering a major-caliber tournament experience for the glittering cast of men's and women's stars it attracts every year. It's the incomparable "Beijing Experience", though, that sets it apart from the others in the same category, with international players presented with cultural experience trips or events to explore the Chinese capital's timeless heritage, folk customs and modern trends. It's a treat that suits 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic perfectly, with the Serbian great, known for his inner strength and serenity when facing fierce on-court battles, rejuvenated after a pre-tournament visit to the Summer Palace, an imperial park in the northwestern Beijing suburbs known for its ancient grandeur and tranquility. After taking a walk around the Kunming Lake to savor the serene ambiance of the park, Djokovic spent some time experiencing two quintessential Chinese traditions. First, he tried his hand at water calligraphy by learning how to write the Chinese characters of his name with a big brush pen on the ground.

item.title: Nation tops Asian Games table for 12th time
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Nation tops Asian Games table for 12th time China retained the top spot for a record 12th consecutive time as the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games drew to a close on Sunday, creating another record with the number of gold medals won and introducing to the world a new generation of promising Chinese athletes. The Chinese competitors won 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals, a total haul of 341 medals, surpassing the previous record of 165 golds won in an overseas Asian Games set in 2006 at Doha, Qatar. Japan finished second with 83 golds, followed by the Republic of Korea with 39. Beyond the medal haul, the Games also provided a platform for a new generation of sporting talents. China's 13-year-old swimming sensation Yu Zidi was named the Most Valuable Player among females, while Thailand's 20-year-old sprinter Puripol Boonson won in the men's category. Yu won gold in all three of her individual events, setting Games records in each, including an Asian record. Boonson completed a sprint double, winning the men's 100m in a Games record of 9.90 seconds and the 200m in 19.88, equaling the Asian record. "Tonight, we close a Games that will shape the next generation of Asian sport," Olympic Council of Asia President Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani said in his closing ceremony speech. Athletes set 54 world records and 89 Asian records during the Games, OCA Director General Husain Al Musallam said. He said the Games had continued to unite Asia through sport despite conflicts and economic instability around the world. "Asia is united in sport, in peace and in solidarity," he said. "This is our aim."
